items.name: Daily check: symptoms, sleep and mood
items.plain: Answer three short questions each day: anything new in your body, how you slept, and how your mood is.
items.why: Small changes are easiest to catch early, and astronauts often sleep less than they need. Your own answers, day after day, build the baseline that every other reading is compared with.
items.instrument: The app; the wrist band offers a sleep estimate that you confirm or correct
steps: Open Today and tap Daily check.
Symptoms: tap the body area if something is new or worse. If nothing is new, tap Nothing new.
Sleep: look at the wrist band estimate. Keep it if it is right, or change it. Your correction is saved next to the band's number, which is never erased.
Mood: move the slider to how you feel right now. There is no right answer.
If anything feels urgent, press Someone needs help instead of finishing the check.
The check is done when these three questions are answered. Other readings are optional.

items.name: Resting pulse
items.plain: Sit still for a few minutes and let the camera station read your pulse, or count it at your wrist.
items.why: Your resting pulse is a simple sign of how your heart and body are coping. A change from your own usual number can point to illness, dehydration, poor sleep or stress.
items.instrument: Camera station (experimental, compared against the oximeter); kit pulse oximeter; or two fingers and a watch
steps: Rest quietly for 10 minutes first. Do not take it right after exercise.
Camera station: hold still facing the cameras in good light until the reading appears. If it says No reading, keep still and try once more.
By hand: place your index and middle finger on the inside of the opposite wrist, below the base of the thumb, and press gently until you feel the beat.
Count the beats for 1 full minute, or for 30 seconds and multiply by 2.
Never press on both sides of the neck at the same time.
Save the number. The app compares it with your own usual range.

items.name: Breathing rate
items.plain: Sit quietly and let the camera station count your breaths for a minute, or have a crewmate count them.
items.why: How fast you breathe at rest changes early with lung problems, fever, anxiety and bad air. It is hard to count your own breaths honestly, so a camera or a crewmate does it better.
items.instrument: Camera station (experimental); or a crewmate and a watch
steps: Sit somewhere quiet and relax for a few minutes.
Breathe normally. Do not try to control it.
Camera station: hold still until the reading appears.
By hand: a crewmate watches your chest rise and fall and counts the breaths for 60 seconds.
Save the number with who or what counted it.

items.name: Blood pressure
items.plain: Rest, then take two or three cuff readings one minute apart on your upper arm.
items.why: Spaceflight shifts body fluids toward the head and changes how blood pressure is controlled. High blood pressure usually causes no symptoms, so it is only found by measuring.
items.instrument: Kit blood pressure cuff (upper arm)
steps: Empty your bladder. No food, caffeine or exercise in the last 30 minutes.
Rest for at least 5 minutes, 10 is better. In weightlessness, use foot loops or a strap to hold a seated posture with your back against a support.
Bare your upper arm. Keep the arm supported at heart level.
Wrap the cuff snugly. Its lower edge sits about 2.5 cm above the bend of your elbow.
Press start and stay still and quiet while it measures.
Take 2 or 3 readings, 1 minute apart. Save all of them with the time.

raise_frequency_when.trigger: Headache, dizziness, fainting, or a change in vision

new_cadence.note: measure now, then daily for 3 days

items.name: Blood oxygen (pulse oximeter)
items.plain: Clip the pulse oximeter on a warm finger, keep still, and save the steady number.
items.why: Blood oxygen shows whether your lungs are getting oxygen into your blood. It matters most when breathing feels wrong or the cabin air or pressure changes.
items.instrument: Kit pulse oximeter (finger)
steps: Warm and relax your hand. Remove any nail polish from that finger.
Clip the oximeter on the finger. Keep the hand below heart level.
Keep still. Do not move that hand.
Wait until the number stops changing and shows one steady value.
Save the number with the time. The app also saves the pulse the oximeter shows, to check the camera.

raise_frequency_when.trigger: Shortness of breath, bluish lips or nails, chest tightness, or a racing pulse

items.name: Body temperature
items.plain: Take your temperature under the tongue with the digital thermometer when you feel unwell, and at the monthly exam.
items.why: A raised temperature is usually a sign of infection. In a closed habitat, one person's infection can spread to the whole crew.
items.instrument: Kit digital thermometer
steps: Wait 30 minutes after eating, drinking or exercise.
Clean the tip with soap and water, then rinse it.
Turn it on and put the tip under your tongue, towards the back of your mouth.
Close your lips around it and wait until it beeps or flashes.
Save the number and say where you measured (mouth or armpit).
If you feel hot, cold or shivery, report it even if the number looks normal.

items.name: Body mass
items.plain: Measure your body mass on the habitat's mass device at the same time of day each week.
items.why: Crews often eat less than they need in flight, and losing mass can mean losing muscle and bone. Tracking it shows early whether you are eating enough.
items.instrument: Mass measurement device (ISS class, for example SLAMMD); not in this kit
steps: Measure at the same time of day each week, before eating and after using the toilet.
Wear the same light clothing each time.
Follow the device's own instructions to the end.
Save the number and the device used.
On the Moon or Mars, a scale made for Earth reads weight, not mass, and reads low. Use the device the habitat provides for mass.

items.name: Fluids and hydration
items.plain: Log roughly how much you drank today and the colour of your urine.
items.why: Dehydration causes headache, poor sleep and poor performance, raises the risk of kidney stones and urinary infection, and raises the risk of decompression sickness on a spacewalk.
items.instrument: The app; drink bags or the water dispenser count
steps: Tap how much you drank today, in drink bags or litres.
Pick the urine colour that matches best. Pale is the goal.
Tick if you feel thirsty, or are passing urine less often than usual.
If your urine is dark or you feel thirsty, drink now and check again later.

items.name: Exercise session and log
items.plain: Do your prescribed exercise and log what you did, how long, and anything that hurt.
items.why: Without gravity, muscle, bone and heart fitness fall. Daily exercise is the main protection, and you need that strength to walk, egress and work after landing.
items.instrument: Habitat exercise devices; wrist band for activity and pulse; the app log
steps: Do the session your strength and conditioning team prescribed.
Log the device, minutes and how hard it felt.
Note any pain, joint trouble or dizziness. Do not push through sharp pain.
If you missed a session, log the reason. A missed session is never filled in for you.

items.name: Reaction test (PVT-B, 3 minutes)
items.plain: Tap the screen as fast as you can each time the counter appears, for 3 minutes.
items.why: Tiredness slows your reactions before you notice it yourself. This short test is the same kind NASA used on the ISS and shows when sleep loss is affecting you.
items.instrument: The app reaction test (PVT-B style); a quiet spot
steps: Find a quiet spot where you will not be interrupted for 4 minutes.
Answer the short questions on how tired, stressed and sleepy you feel.
Watch the box. When the counter appears, tap as fast as you can.
Do not tap before it appears. Early taps count as errors.
Keep going until the 3 minutes end. The app compares the result with your own usual speed.
Note any distraction during the test.

items.name: Monthly thinking test (WinSCAT class)
items.plain: Once a month, take the longer computer thinking test that ISS crews use, so changes after an injury or illness can be judged.
items.why: A monthly result gives a known baseline. If someone hits their head or becomes ill, the crew can compare and see how much thinking is affected and whether it recovers.
items.instrument: Cognitive test software such as WinSCAT, if the vehicle carries it; not in this kit
steps: Pick a quiet time when you are not rushed.
Start the test and follow its on-screen instructions.
Finish all parts in one sitting.
The result goes to the ground team, who compare it with your pre-flight baseline.

raise_frequency_when.trigger: A head injury, or an illness that affects thinking

items.name: Vision self-check: near reading card and Amsler grid
items.plain: Read the near card and look at the Amsler grid, one eye at a time, and note anything blurred, wavy or missing.
items.why: Long missions can change the shape of the eye and blur near vision (SANS). Most crew on long flights show some signs, and the risk grows with time in space. A quick self-check finds changes between the formal eye exams.
items.instrument: Near reading card and Amsler grid card (paper or on screen at a fixed size)
steps: Wear the glasses you normally use for reading. Use good light.
Hold the card at your usual reading distance; for the Amsler grid, 30 to 38 cm.
Cover one eye.
Near card: read the smallest line you can and save it.
Amsler grid: look straight at the centre dot. Without moving your eye, notice whether any lines look blurry, wavy, dark or missing.
Repeat with the other eye.
Answer the short vision questions: blurred near vision, headaches, eye pain.

items.name: SANS eye exam (OCT, fundoscopy, ultrasound)
items.plain: On scheduled eye weeks, a trained crewmate images your eyes while a ground expert guides by video.
items.why: Swelling at the back of the eye and folds in the retina cannot be seen in a self-check. Only imaging shows them, and they may not cause symptoms early.
items.instrument: OCT, fundoscope, ocular ultrasound, where the vehicle has them; not in this kit
steps: The trained operator sets up the device and opens the video link to the ground guide.
Follow the operator's instructions for where to look and when to keep still.
The ground team checks image quality while you are still in position.
Do the ocular questionnaire, visual acuity and Amsler grid in the same session.
Results are reviewed by the ground; the app records the exam as an imported report.

items.name: Hearing check (on-orbit hearing assessment)
items.plain: Take the headphone hearing test in a quiet spot so flight surgeons can see any change in your hearing.
items.why: Habitat fans and equipment are noisy all day and night. Hearing can shift without you noticing, and ISS tests have found shifts in many crewmembers.
items.instrument: Audiometer with headphones (ISS class, for example the on-orbit hearing assessment kit); not in this kit. Without it, the hearing questions in the daily check
steps: Go to the quietest place in the habitat. Switch off nearby fans you are allowed to switch off.
Put on the test headphones and follow the instructions.
Press the button each time you hear a tone, even a very faint one.
Test both ears.
The result goes to the ground for review.

items.name: Crew-worn noise dosimeter (24 hours)
items.plain: Wear the small noise monitor on your clothing for a full day and night, then hand it in for download.
items.why: People get used to noise and stop noticing it, but it still harms hearing and sleep. Only a measurement shows your real exposure and whether you need hearing protection.
items.instrument: Acoustic dosimeter (ISS class); not in this kit. Habitat sound level sensors run continuously
steps: Before breakfast, clip the monitor to your clothing near your shoulder and start it.
Wear it all day. Do not cover the microphone.
Just before sleep, a crewmate swaps its battery and gives it back to you.
Keep it on through the night, near your head.
In the morning, stop it before your normal activities and hand it in.
Wear your hearing protection as usual. The app notes when you wore it.

items.name: Personal radiation dosimeter
items.plain: Wear your dosimeter at all times, check each day that it is on and working, and read it before and after every spacewalk.
items.why: Space radiation cannot be felt. Your dosimeter keeps your personal dose record, and an alarm tells everyone when to take shelter during a solar storm.
items.instrument: Personal dosimeter (ISS class); habitat radiation monitor with alarm; not in this kit
steps: Wear the dosimeter where the program tells you, inside the habitat and during spacewalks.
Each day, tap to confirm it is on you and working.
Before and after each spacewalk, read it and save the number.
If the radiation alarm sounds, go to the shelter area at once and follow the shelter procedure.
During a shelter period, read your dosimeter when asked and save each reading.

items.name: Before a spacewalk
items.plain: In the day before a spacewalk, do a short health check and a private talk with the flight surgeon, who must clear you.
items.why: A spacewalk is hard physical work in a pressurized suit. A cold, short sleep, dehydration or an injury can turn into a real problem outside, so each person is cleared first by the medical officer aboard, as in the onboard procedure.
items.instrument: Kit cuff, oximeter, thermometer, camera station; reaction test; personal dosimeter
steps: Answer the pre-spacewalk questions: new symptoms, ear or sinus problems, sleep, pain, mood.
Take pulse, blood pressure, blood oxygen and temperature.
Drink to stay well hydrated, as prescribed.
Check your hands: trim nails short and note any sore fingertips or nails.
Read and save your dosimeter.

The medical officer clears you before suiting up, as in the onboard procedure. When the link is up, also join the private medical conference within 24 hours before; the flight surgeon's advice goes into that decision. Log it for the ground.

transit.note: contingency spacewalks only

lunar_surface.note: surface walks may be frequent; one check per walk

mars_surface.note: the ground's reply is delayed; the medical officer clears each person aboard, and the log goes at the next contact

items.name: After a spacewalk: bends, hands, shoulders
items.plain: After the suit comes off, check for signs of the bends, look at your hands and nails, note shoulder pain, and talk privately with the flight surgeon within a day.
items.why: Decompression sickness (the bends) can start hours after a spacewalk, and people tend to play down mild symptoms. Gloves often injure fingertips and nails, and suits strain shoulders.
items.instrument: The app; kit oximeter and cuff; camera of the tablet for hand photos; personal dosimeter
steps: Report at once, never wait: joint or muscle pain, itching, a blotchy rash, numbness, tingling, weakness, dizziness, trouble thinking, or trouble breathing.
If any of these appear, press Someone needs help. Do not do hard exercise.
Look at each finger and nail. Note lifted or dark nails, blisters, sore knuckles or numb fingertips. Take a photo if asked.
Move each shoulder through its full range. Note pain or catching.
Take pulse and blood oxygen. Read and save your dosimeter.
On the Moon or Mars, also do the dust check.
Join the private medical conference within 24 hours.

items.name: Eyes, skin and breathing after dust exposure
items.plain: After a surface walk or any dust in the cabin, rinse your eyes if they sting, check your skin and nails, and note any sneezing, congestion or cough.
items.why: Moon and Mars dust is sharp and clings to everything. Apollo crews got sore eyes, blocked noses and dust in the cabin. Mars dust also carries chemicals such as perchlorate.
items.instrument: Eyewash, saline, wipes; the app; habitat dust monitor
steps: Clean dust off yourself and your gear before entering the living area, as the procedure says.
If your eyes sting or feel gritty, do not rub them. Rinse with the eyewash or saline.
Look at your skin, under your nails and around the wrists for redness or scratches.
Note sneezing, blocked nose, sore throat or cough.
Take your breathing rate if you are coughing.
Tell the crew medical officer about any eye pain that stays after rinsing.

items.name: Weekly wellbeing self-check
items.plain: Once a week, rate sleep, tiredness, workload, morale, relationships and mood, privately, to bring to your private conferences.
items.why: Isolation, workload and distance from home wear people down slowly. The same topics flight psychologists ask about every two weeks help you notice changes yourself.
items.instrument: The app (private; never shared without your choice)
steps: Find a private moment.
Rate each topic: sleep, tiredness, workload, your morale, the crew's morale, relationships with the crew and the ground, mood, family and personal life, and the habitat (food, noise, space).
Add a note if you want. It stays private.
Choose whether to share any of it at your next private conference.
If you have thoughts of harming yourself, press Someone needs help now.

items.why: It is the routine way to raise anything about your health in private, and for the flight surgeon to check in before and after demanding events.

items.name: Private psychological conference
items.plain: A private, unrecorded talk with the flight psychologist or psychiatrist every two weeks.
items.why: Living and working in a small crew far from home is hard. A regular private talk helps with sleep, stress, relationships and family worries before they grow.

items.name: Monthly health exam (periodic health status)
items.plain: Once a month, the crew medical officer examines you and records your vital signs and ear images for the flight surgeon.
items.why: A regular exam by a trained crewmate catches things you would not notice yourself and gives the flight surgeon a consistent record to compare.
items.instrument: Kit cuff, oximeter, thermometer; otoscope and exam form (ISS class)
steps: The crew medical officer opens the exam form in the app.
Pulse, blood pressure, temperature and blood oxygen are taken as in their own items.
The officer looks in each ear with the otoscope and saves the images.
You answer the exam questions; the officer fills in what they see.
The exam is sent to the flight surgeon, who compares it with earlier exams and replies.

new_cadence.note: as the crew medical officer decides

items.name: Mouth, teeth and skin check
items.plain: Once a month, look at your teeth, gums and skin with a mirror and light, and note anything new.
items.why: Dental abscesses and skin rashes have happened on the ISS. Far from a dentist, a small problem found early is easier to manage.
items.instrument: Mirror, penlight; tablet camera for photos
steps: Look at your gums and teeth. Note bleeding, swelling, a broken tooth or a sore that will not heal.
Note any tooth pain, especially with hot or cold.
Look over your skin, including feet and under straps. Note rashes, sores, dry cracked skin or a changing mole.
Ask a crewmate to look at your back.
Take a photo of anything new and save it.

raise_frequency_when.trigger: Tooth pain, facial swelling or a gum problem

new_cadence.note: tell the crew medical officer now

raise_frequency_when.trigger: A rash or skin sore

new_cadence.note: photo each day until it clears; crew medical officer decides

items.name: Medicines and medical kit check
items.plain: Once a month, check that the medical kit is complete, in date and stowed where the list says.
items.why: In an emergency there is no time to search. On long missions without resupply, medicines can pass their expiry dates, so the crew needs to know early what is running out.
items.instrument: Medical kits; the inventory list in the app
steps: Open the kit list in the app.
Check each emergency item first: present, sealed, working.
Check expiry dates. Flag anything expiring before the next resupply or the end of the mission.
Check that used items were logged and replaced.
Check that personal medicines match each person's list.
Send the flags to the ground.

transit.note: no resupply; expiry planning matters more

mars_surface.note: no resupply; expiry planning matters more

raise_frequency_when.trigger: Any item is used from a kit

new_cadence.note: log and restock the same day

raise_frequency_when.trigger: A resupply arrives

new_cadence.note: unpack and update the list

raise_frequency_when.trigger: A solar particle event

new_cadence.note: check liquid medicines for changes and log it for the ground

items.name: Medical emergency drill
items.plain: Practise a medical emergency as a crew: who does what, where the kit is, and how to use the Someone needs help screen.
items.why: Skills fade between training and a real emergency, which may come months later. A drill keeps everyone ready, not only the medical officer.
items.instrument: Emergency medical kit; the app's Someone needs help screen in drill mode
steps: The crew medical officer picks a scenario from the drill list.
One person plays the patient. Another presses Someone needs help in drill mode.
Run the fixed emergency steps. Fetch and open the real kit.
Practise each skill with its teach steps and camera checks: the pulse check on a crewmate's real wrist, chest compressions on a manikin, if listed. The camera's numbers show live and are not stored.
Practise the log for the ground: preview it and press Tell the ground. It leaves at the next contact, and nothing in the drill waits for it.
Debrief: what was slow, what was missing. Log it. Completing the drill updates each participant's skill record and counts toward the practice patches.

raise_frequency_when.trigger: A new module or a visiting vehicle

new_cadence.note: emergency response review

raise_frequency_when.trigger: After a real medical emergency

new_cadence.note: debrief and repeat the drill

items.name: Drinking water sampling
items.plain: Once a month, take a water sample from the dispenser with the sampling kit and process or stow it as the procedure says.
items.why: Recycled water can grow bacteria. Regular samples catch a problem before people get sick.
items.instrument: Water sampling kit (ISS class, for example microbial capture device and coliform test); not in this kit. The habitat water quality sensor runs continuously
steps: Collect the sample from the dispenser port named in the procedure. Alternate hot and ambient ports month to month.
Label it with date, time and port.
Process it with the kit or stow it for return, as the procedure says.
Log the sample and any result in the app.

transit.note: team default, same as ISS

lunar_surface.note: team default, same as ISS

mars_surface.note: plus after any change of water source; local water may carry perchlorate

raise_frequency_when.trigger: The water quality sensor approaches a limit (sensor_limit)

new_cadence.note: sample now

raise_frequency_when.trigger: Water tastes, smells or looks different, or several crew have stomach upsets

new_cadence.event: change in the water, or stomach upsets
new_cadence.note: sample now and log it for the ground

raise_frequency_when.trigger: A count above limits

new_cadence.note: until two clean results

items.name: Cabin air sampling
items.plain: Every three months, run the microbial air sampler in each module, and take an air sample before the return trip.
items.why: Moulds and bacteria in the air can cause infections and allergies in a closed cabin. A return air sample records what the crew breathed.
items.instrument: Microbial air sampler kit and air sample containers (ISS class); not in this kit. Habitat CO2, oxygen and trace gas sensors run continuously
steps: Take the air sampler to each module on the list.
Run it for the time the procedure sets, away from vents.
Label and stow each sample plate or container.
Log the module, time and any smell or visible growth.

station_leo.note: microbial air sampling; plus a return air sample

transit.note: microbial air sampling; plus a return air sample

lunar_surface.note: microbial air sampling; plus a return air sample

mars_surface.note: microbial air sampling; plus a return air sample

raise_frequency_when.trigger: A strange smell, smoke, a chemical leak or a contamination event

new_cadence.note: sample as the ground directs

raise_frequency_when.trigger: Before the vehicle's return trip

new_cadence.note: return air sample

raise_frequency_when.trigger: A count above limits, or visible mould

new_cadence.note: until clean

items.name: Surface microbial sampling
items.plain: Every three months, press sample slides or swabs on the listed surfaces and stow them.
items.why: Surfaces people touch carry germs between crewmembers and can grow mould, especially where it is damp.
items.instrument: Surface sampler kit, contact slides and swabs (ISS class); not in this kit
steps: Go to each surface on the list.
Press a contact slide on flat surfaces. Use a wetted swab on uneven ones.
Label and stow each sample.
Log where you sampled and anything you saw, such as damp or growth.

raise_frequency_when.trigger: Visible mould, damp or condensation

new_cadence.note: sample and clean

raise_frequency_when.trigger: A count above limits, or several crew with skin or stomach infections

new_cadence.note: until clean

items.name: Weekly cleaning
items.plain: Once a week, the crew cleans surfaces, handholds and corners together.
items.why: Cleaning keeps germs and mould down in a closed habitat. On the Moon or Mars it also removes dust tracked in from outside.
items.instrument: Vacuum, disinfectant wipes, towels
steps: Split the habitat into areas, one per person.
Wipe handholds, tables, switches and the toilet area with disinfectant.
Vacuum filters, vents and corners where things collect.
Report damp spots, growth or dust build-up in the app.

lunar_surface.note: plus dust cleaning after each surface walk

mars_surface.note: plus dust cleaning after each surface walk

raise_frequency_when.trigger: Dust brought in after a surface walk

new_cadence.note: clean the entry area

raise_frequency_when.trigger: Visible growth or a spill

items.name: Pre-flight baselines
items.plain: Before launch, use the app on the ground so it learns your usual readings, and record the baseline tests the medical team does.
items.why: Every in-flight warning compares you with yourself. Without a good baseline from before flight, the app cannot tell what is normal for you.
items.instrument: The whole kit; ground clinic tests imported as reports
steps: Do the daily check every day for at least the last 2 weeks before launch.
Take resting pulse, breathing rate, blood pressure, blood oxygen and temperature several times in those weeks.
Do the reaction test about monthly in the last six months, and more often in the final weeks.
Do the near vision and Amsler grid self-check, and record the eye exam results.
Import the baseline reports: eye exams, hearing test, fitness test, dental exam, cognitive baseline.
Set your medicines, allergies and conditions, or decline each field.

raise_frequency_when.trigger: A baseline reading is missing or failed

new_cadence.note: repeat before launch

items.name: Pre-flight quarantine (health stabilization)
items.plain: In the 14 days before launch, limit contact to approved people and report any sign of illness each day.
items.why: An infection caught just before launch can spread through the whole crew in a closed vehicle. Quarantine and vaccinations cut that risk.
items.instrument: The app daily check; kit thermometer
steps: Follow the quarantine rules: only approved contacts, protective equipment as required.
Do the daily check each day, with temperature.
Report sore throat, cough, fever, stomach upset or a rash the same day.
Report any contact with someone who is ill.

default.note: daily for the 14 days before launch

station_leo.note: daily for the 14 days before launch

transit.note: daily for the 14 days before launch

lunar_surface.note: daily for the 14 days before launch

mars_surface.note: daily for the 14 days before launch

raise_frequency_when.trigger: Any symptom of infection or a known exposure

new_cadence.note: tell the flight surgeon the same day

items.name: First days in space: adaptation check
items.plain: For the first five days, answer a short daily check on nausea, headache, stuffy nose, back pain and passing urine.
items.why: Most people feel sick, congested or sore in the first days as the body adapts to weightlessness. Most of it passes in a few days, but vomiting and not passing urine need help.
items.instrument: The app; the daily private medical conference
steps: Answer each question: nausea or vomiting, headache, stuffy nose or puffy face, back pain, dizziness when you move your head, trouble passing urine, appetite.
Rate how much each one affects your work.
Sip fluids even if you feel sick.
If you cannot pass urine, or keep vomiting, tell the crew medical officer now.
Bring the answers to the daily private medical conference.

transit.note: daily for 5 days after launch

lunar_surface.note: daily for 5 days after launch; see the gravity arrival check for the landing

mars_surface.note: daily for 5 days after launch; see the gravity arrival check for the landing

raise_frequency_when.trigger: Symptoms still present after 5 days

new_cadence.note: until resolved

items.name: After landing on the Moon or Mars: gravity check
items.plain: In the first days after landing on the Moon or Mars, stand up slowly with a crewmate near, and check dizziness, balance, pulse and blood pressure.
items.why: After weeks or months of weightlessness, standing can make you faint and your balance is off. On Mars there is no ground team to help in real time.
items.instrument: Kit cuff and oximeter; camera station; the app
steps: Before standing, sit for a minute. Stand up slowly with a crewmate beside you.
Take pulse and blood pressure lying or sitting, then after standing still for a few minutes, if you feel well enough to stand.
Sit or lie down at once if you feel faint, sweaty or sick.
Note dizziness, nausea, unsteady walking or blurred vision.
Do not start surface walks until the crew medical officer agrees.

default.event: landing on the Moon or Mars

transit.note: not applicable

lunar_surface.note: daily for the first 5 days

mars_surface.note: daily for the first 5 days; longer if the transit was long

raise_frequency_when.trigger: Fainting or near fainting

new_cadence.note: press Someone needs help

items.name: Before return: entry preparation
items.plain: In the last weeks before coming home, do the final eye exam, the daily talks in the last five days, and the fluid loading the flight surgeon prescribes.
items.why: Returning to gravity after a long time in space makes people faint on standing. Drinking a set amount of fluid with salt before entry, and a final check, lower that risk.
items.instrument: Kit cuff, oximeter; eye exam devices where available; fluid and salt tablets from the kit
steps: About 30 days before return: formal eye tests (and imaging if carried).
From five days before entry: daily private medical conference.
Keep up exercise to the end.
Do the pre-landing medical evaluation with the crew medical officer.
Before entry: drink the fluid and salt the flight surgeon prescribed, and note the amount.

transit.note: before Earth entry, and before a Mars landing

lunar_surface.note: before leaving the surface and before Earth entry

mars_surface.note: before leaving the surface; Earth entry follows the return transit

raise_frequency_when.trigger: The five days before entry

items.name: After landing on Earth: recovery checks
items.plain: After landing, follow the medical exams and the daily reconditioning plan, and keep doing the app's short checks on the schedule below.
items.why: Muscles, balance, blood pressure control, eyes and sleep all need weeks to readjust. Regular checks show recovery and catch problems.
items.instrument: The app; ground clinic tests imported as reports
steps: Immediately after landing: medical checks by the recovery team. Accept help to move.
Do not drive or do heavy physical tasks until cleared.
Reconditioning: about 2 hours a day, 7 days a week, for 45 days.
Reaction test: daily for the first week, then 30, 60 and 90 days after landing.
Eye tests in the first days; behavioral health talks around days 3, 14 and 30 to 45; fitness tests at day 7 and day 30.
Keep the daily check going while you recover.

transit.note: after the long transit, recovery may take longer

mars_surface.note: after the longest missions, recovery may take longer

raise_frequency_when.trigger: Fainting, falls, or a new symptom during recovery

new_cadence.note: tell the recovery team

raise_frequency_when.trigger: A long mission

new_cadence.note: extend the plan as the flight surgeon decides
